To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
epidural morphine is more suitable for postoperative pain management than fentanyl.
epidural opioids are the mainstay of pain control after major surgery.

the use of epidural opioids in clinical practice should be based on the following considerations: (a) the type and the severity of the surgical procedure, (b) the type and duration of analgesia required, (c) the type and severity of the side effects expected and (d) the patient s age and comorbidity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
providing the most recent evidence-based information to support the best clinical practice in postoperative pain treatment.
the following questions. Which is the ideal opioid for postoperative pain treatment?
a better understanding of the mechanisms of action of opioids and the pharmacological properties of the most used epidural opioids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best opioid for postoperative pain management is the one that has a good balance between analgesic efficacy and side effect profile.
the choice of the opioid should be made based on the type of surgery, the patient s clinical characteristics and the physician s preference.
lipophilic opioids are more appropriate for short-term postoperative pain management, whereas hydrophilic opioids are more suitable for long-term analgesia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the epidural administration of a hydrophilic opioid like fentanyl is more suitable for short-term analgesia, while morphine can provide longer analgesic effect.

the use of lipophilic opioids like fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil, and more recently remifentanil is recommended for the treatment of postoperative pain, especially in the first 24 h, when an epidural catheter is not left in situ.
the use of lipophilic opioid drugs like fentanyl and sufentanil, in epidural anesthesia, is not recommended because of the high risk of adverse effects and the poor analgesic effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the epidural administration of morphine is a valid choice for postoperative analgesic treatment in patients undergoing major surgery, especially for those with a long postoperative stay in the recovery room, and for the elderly.
the selection of an epidural opioid is based on the clinical indication.
lipophilic opioids are more appropriate to provide a fast onset of analgesia, and hydrophilic opioids are more suitable for long-term analgesia.
